Class DefaultMappings

java.lang.Object
org.openehealth.ipf.commons.map.DefaultMappings
All Implemented Interfaces:
Mappings
Direct Known Subclasses:
SpringMappings
public class DefaultMappings extends Object implements Mappings
In-memory Mappings implementation, backed by one forward and one reverse index per mapping. Both indices are built once, when the mapping is registered, and are never rebuilt afterwards — which is what keeps loading a second mapping source from disturbing the mappings loaded from the first.

Reads are lock-free against an immutable snapshot; registration is serialized, and validates each mapping against what is already registered - which is what lets a lookup follow delegations and composites without checking them again.

This is the extension point for wiring the mapping service into a container: a subclass may add whatever way of naming a source that container prefers and calls load(URL). See SpringMappings in ipf-commons-spring, which takes Spring Resources.

Since:
6.0

    • mappingsFor

      public List<Mapping> mappingsFor(String keySystem, String valueSystem)
      Description copied from interface: Mappings
      Finds mappings by the code systems they translate between, rather than by name.

      A caller holding a code to translate knows which code system it is in and which one it wants, not what the mapping happens to be called - which is the shape of FHIR's ConceptMap/$translate, and the only way to reach a mapping read from a source that names itself, such as a ConceptMap resource. Either argument may be null for "any", so passing only a key system finds every mapping that translates out of it.

      This is a scan over the registered mappings, not an index: resolve the mapping once and keep it, rather than calling this per message.

      Specified by:
      mappingsFor in interface Mappings
      Parameters:
      keySystem - identifier of the key code system, or null for any
      valueSystem - identifier of the value code system, or null for any
      Returns:
      the matching mappings, in registration order

    • translate

      public Optional<Translation> translate(String mapping, String key)
      Description copied from interface: Mappings
      Maps a key like Mappings.map(String, String), and says which code system the answer belongs to and how it is displayed - what a caller needs to build a coded value from it.

      The system is that of the mapping which actually answered: a composite answers with the system of the part that had the answer, a delegating fallback with that of the mapping delegated to. An identity fallback answers with the key itself, and so with the key system.

      The default implementation knows none of that and answers with the mapping's value system and no display; DefaultMappings overrides it.

      Specified by:
      translate in interface Mappings
      Parameters:
      mapping - mapping name
      key - left side of the mapping
      Returns:
      the mapped value with its system and display, falling back to the mapping's unmatched behavior

    • keys

      public Set<String> keys(String mapping)
      Specified by:
      keys in interface Mappings
      Parameters:
      mapping - mapping name
      Returns:
      the keys this mapping translates, in declaration order. A key declared only by a Equivalence.DISJOINT entry is not among them, because it does not translate. The keys of a mapping this one delegates to follow its own, since a lookup asks that mapping for every key this one does not declare; keys that only a fallback such as identity answers are not listed. For a composite they are the keys of all its parts. Changes to the set do not change the mapping

    • setAllowOverride

      public void setAllowOverride(boolean allowOverride)

    • setAllowReverseCollisions

      public void setAllowReverseCollisions(boolean allowReverseCollisions)
      Whether a mapping may register two invertible entries sharing a value, in which case the last one declared wins the reverse index. Off by default: a value with two inverses is a load-time error, since the alternative is a reverse lookup that silently answers whichever key happened to be written last.
